title: Direct Estimation
text:
Direct estimation is the design-based starting point for the SAE workflow. At this stage, each MSOA-year estimate is calculated only from the survey respondents observed in that MSOA and wave, using the matched survey weight.

library(readr)
library(stringr)
library(tidyr)
library(sf)
library(ggplot2)
library(patchwork)

base_path <- here::here("data")
msoa_boundaries <- st_read(
  file.path(base_path, "boundaries-msoa.geojson"),
  quiet = TRUE
) |>
  rename(domain_id = all_of("MSOA21CD")) |>
  filter(str_starts(.data$domain_id, "W"))

domain_frame <- read_csv(
  file.path(base_path, "clean", "msoa_year_domain_frame.csv"),
  show_col_types = FALSE
) |>
  transmute(
    domain_id = .data$domain_id,
    wave_year = .data$wave_year,
    msoa_name = .data$msoa_name

We use survey::svyby() to compute the weighted share and its uncertainty diagnostics for every MSOA-year cell with usable observations. It then completes the MSOA-by-wave grid so missing cells are retained for modelling.

# Define survey design
walk_design <- survey::svydesign(
  ids = stats::as.formula("~1"),
  strata = stats::as.formula("~strata"),
  weights = stats::as.formula("~weight"),
  data = survey_walk
)

# Calculate direct estimate and uncertainty
direct_walk_estimates <- survey::svyby(
  formula = stats::as.formula("~indicator"),
  by = stats::as.formula("~domain_id + wave_year"),
  design = walk_design,
  FUN = survey::svymean,
  vartype = "se",
  na.rm = TRUE,
  keep.names = FALSE
) |>
  tibble::as_tibble() |>
  transmute(
    domain_id = .data$domain_id,
    wave_year = .data$wave_year,
    direct_estimate = .data$indicator,
    standard_error = .data$se
  ) |>
  mutate(variance = .data$standard_error^2)

# Calculate sample size per MSOA-year
direct_walk_counts <- survey_walk |>
  group_by(across(all_of(c("domain_id", "wave_year")))) |>
  summarise(n = dplyr::n(), .groups = "drop")

# Join
direct_walk <- domain_frame |>
  left_join(direct_walk_estimates, by = c(
    "domain_id", "wave_year"
  )) |>
  left_join(direct_walk_counts, by = c(
    "domain_id", "wave_year"
  )) |>
  mutate(n = replace_na(.data$n, 0L))

title: Direct Estimation
text:
2 Evaluate direct estimates
Direct estimation provides a useful starting point because they make three limitations visible:

Uneven temporal and spatial coverage: The number of usable observations varies across survey waves and across MSOAs. This means some MSOA-year estimates are based on much less direct evidence than others.
Unstable area estimate over time: For some MSOAs, direct estimates change sharply between waves. These changes may reflect real behavioural change, but they may also reflect sampling noise.
Zero within-area variance: For binary indicators, especially with small samples, some MSOAs show no within-area variation because all respondents give the same response. This can produce zero or unreliable variance estimates.



Code
# Plotting functions
base_map <- function(wave) {
  wave_direct <- direct_walk[direct_walk[["wave_year"]] == wave, ]

  wave_data <- msoa_boundaries |>
    left_join(wave_direct, by = "domain_id")

  ggplot(wave_data) +
    theme_void() +
    theme(axis.title.y = element_text(angle = 90, margin = margin(r = 15)))
}

plot_estimate <- function(wave) {
  base_map(wave) +
    geom_sf(aes(fill = .data$direct_estimate), colour = "transparent") +
    scale_fill_distiller(
      palette = "Blues", direction = 1, limits = c(0, 1),
      labels = scales::label_percent(accuracy = 1),
      na.value = "grey85"
    )
}

plot_uncertainty <- function(wave) {
  base_map(wave) +
    geom_sf(aes(fill = .data$variance), colour = "transparent") +
    scale_fill_distiller(
      palette = "Oranges",
      direction = 1,
      na.value = "grey85",
      limits = c(0, max(direct_walk$variance, na.rm = TRUE)),
      labels = scales::label_number(accuracy = 0.001),
      name = "Variance"
    )
}

plot_sample <- function(wave) {
  base_map(wave) +
    geom_sf(aes(fill = .data$n), colour = "transparent") +
    scale_fill_gradient(
      low = "#fff8e1",
      high = "#4f3b10",
      limits = c(0, max(direct_walk$n, na.rm = TRUE)),
      na.value = "grey85",
      name = ""
    )
}


# Generate and assemble plots
e_21 <- plot_estimate("2021") +
  ggtitle("2021") +
  ylab("Direct estimate") +
  theme(legend.position = "none")
e_23 <- plot_estimate("2023") +
  ggtitle("2023") +
  theme(legend.position = "none")
e_25 <- plot_estimate("2025") + ggtitle("2025")

u_21 <- plot_uncertainty("2021") +

  theme(legend.position = "none")
u_23 <- plot_uncertainty("2023") + theme(legend.position = "none")
u_25 <- plot_uncertainty("2025")

title: Spatio-Temporal Bayesian Small Area Estimation for Urban Analytics
text:
[draft] Beginner-friendly Small Area Estimation (SAE) for researchers estimating survey-derived metrics across a whole country or region at fine geographic resolution.
The site has two tracks: a theory track that explains the SAE workflow, and a practical tutorial track that applies the workflow to a dataset. It uses the National Survey for Wales as the first worked survey.
The main practical uses R, Quarto, and SAE packages such as survey, INLA. Make sure you have latest R version installed.

title: Spatio-Temporal Bayesian Small Area Estimation for Urban Analytics
text:
1 Why Small Area Estimation?
[draft] Survey are often not precise enough for fine geographies such as Local Authorities, MSOAs, or LSOAs. Some areas have very few/no respondents, unequal weights Taking weighted meands can be unstable. Also out of domain sample
SAE is useful when direct estimates are too noisy or incomplete. Area-level SAE use direct estimates and their sampling variances, borrow strength across areas using covariates and random effects.
SAE can be further improved with bayesian statistics (to smooth out area) and add spatial structure (spatial autocorrelation)
SAE combines survey data, population estimates, auxiliary data, modelling to estimate the unsurveyed in an informed way.

Modelling Data Preparation
text: This workbook introduces the survey source, defines the estimand, documents the synthetic geography, and explains the analysis-ready data products used by the estimation workflows that follow.

title: Modelling Data Preparation
section: 1 Synthetic National Survey for Wales response datasets - 3 waves
text:
1 Synthetic National Survey for Wales response datasets - 3 waves
The tutorial uses a synthetic teaching dataset based on the National Survey for Wales (NSW). The NSW is a repeated cross-sectional survey of people in Wales, with annual survey periods covering topics such as transport, health, education, public services, housing, internet access, climate change, and the Welsh language. For this tutorial, the cleaned microdata combine three survey periods: 2020-2021, 2022-2023, and 2024-2025 into one harmonised survey microdata.
Since the survey responses are geo-indexed at the Local Authority level, but the practical tutorial estimates indicators at MSOA level, we use a synthetic MSOA assignment. The cleaned survey file keeps each respondent’s Local Authority and assigns a synthetic MSOA within that Local Authority using deterministic random allocation. As such, estimates produced from these data should not be read as substantive findings about individual MSOAs in Wales.
This design has two purposes:

Higher spatial resolution for tutorial purposes. The tutorial can demonstrate MSOA-level direct estimation, area-level SAE, spatial modelling, and MRP-style poststratification.
Privacy and disclosure protection. The assigned MSOA is not the respondent’s true MSOA, so the tutorial avoids presenting fine-grained respondent locations.




Synthetic areal disaggregation





Preparation pipeline for analysis-ready inputs

title: Modelling Data Preparation
text:
2 Defining the Estimand
It is important to define the estimand before proceeding to the next step. The estimand determines how we can formulate the appropraite indicator from survey variables, how we aggregate it to the desired area level, and which model inputs such as predictors and spatio-temporal structure are valid downstream. A well-formed estimand answers:

Estimate the measure of what outcome, among which population, across which geography and time period.

For the main tutorial, we use seek to perform SAE on estimand:

Choice




Measure

Outcome
Walks for transport daily


Target population
Adults


Geography

The target population definition is particularly important when we are estimating means or proportions since it determines the denominator for such aggregation. Moreover, it dictates the requirement for target population sizes or poststratification tables when formulating the models.

title: Modelling Data Preparation
text:
4 Preparing auxiliary data

4.1 Area Predictors
Area-level SAE needs covariates that plausibly explain spatial differences in daily walking. The area predictors drawn from Census 2021 bulk tables at MSOA level. The table keeps raw variables for interpretation and z-scored cov_* variables for modelling.
These variables are chosen because daily walking is likely to vary with density, car access, commuting mode, housing form, and the socioeconomic and student composition of each area.







Variables
Why include




Population density
Denser urban areas tend to be more walkable


Share of households without car/van
Individual no-car households tend to walk, cycle, take public transport more


Working from home, Full-time students and routine/semi-routine occupations
Individual occupation may explain their propensity to walk





4.2 Poststratification Table
A population poststratification table is needed to apply the fitted unit-level model to the target population. Because the estimand is the share of adults who walk for transport daily, the tutorial uses an MSOA-by-year-by-age-by-sex population table.
We built our poststratification tables from ONS MSOA quinary age-by-sex population estimates and keeps the survey years used in this tutorial: 2021, 2023, and 2025. A few notes on the preparation of the poststratification tables:

The youngest available ONS age band is 15 to 19. This is used as the closest available population cell for the 16+ walking estimand.
For MRP, the variables that define poststratification cells must be available in both the survey and the population table, with compatible categories.

Note that other useful predictors can still enter the unit-level model as area-level predictors. For example, population density and no-car households are joined by MSOA. They help explain spatial differences in walking, but they do not need to define additional poststratification cells.

Meaning

Before fitting the models, we create a consistent numeric index for each MSOA and survey year. These indices are used by INLA to attach random effects to the correct area and period.

area_levels <- sort(unique(model_data_raw[["domain_id"]]))
year_levels <- sort(unique(model_data_raw[["wave_year"]]))

area_index <- tibble::tibble(
  domain_id = area_levels,
  area_id = seq_along(area_levels)
)

year_index <- tibble::tibble(
  wave_year = year_levels,
  year_id = seq_along(year_levels)
)

To include a spatial random effect, we also need an adjacency graph .adj as input. We use Queen contiguity, where two MSOAs are treated as neighbours if their boundaries touch at either an edge or a point. The boundary file is sorted using area_index so that the graph order matches the area IDs used in the modelling data.


msoa_boundaries_sorted <- msoa_boundaries |>
  dplyr::inner_join(area_index, by = "domain_id") |>
  dplyr::arrange(.data$area_id)

msoa_neighbours <- spdep::poly2nb(
  msoa_boundaries_sorted,
  queen = TRUE,
  row.names = msoa_boundaries_sorted$domain_id
)

spatial_graph_file <- tempfile(fileext = ".adj")

spdep::nb2INLA(
  file = spatial_graph_file,
  nb = msoa_neighbours
)

We then assemble the modelling data. The models use two area-level random-effect structures, so we create separate INLA index variables:

area_iid_id indexes the unstructured, independent area effect.
area_spatial_id indexes the structured spatial area effect, which uses the adjacency graph.

Lastly, the sampling variance also needs careful handling before fitting the FH models with INLA, because the extent to which the noisy direct estimates will be stablised depends on their sampling variances.

Because the outcome is binary (1 for walking daily, 0 otherwise), small MSOA-year samples can produce direct estimates with very low or zero variance. If untreated, these MSOA-year small areas would be treated by the model as overly precise. To avoid this, we apply a minimum sampling variance floor that is the 5% quantile.
For MSOA-year small areas without a direct estimate and as a result no variance, we assign maximum sampling variance, signalling the high uncertainty. Their estimates will be the model prediction.


sampling_variance_floor <- quantile(
  model_data_raw$variance[model_data_raw$variance > 0],
  probs = 0.05,
  na.rm = TRUE,
  names = FALSE
)

sampling_variance_ceiling <- max(
  model_data_raw$variance[model_data_raw$variance > 0],
  na.rm = TRUE
)

model_data <- model_data_raw |>
  left_join(area_index, by = "domain_id") |>
  left_join(year_index, by = "wave_year") |>
  mutate(
    area_iid_id = area_id,
    area_spatial_id = area_id,
    sampling_variance = case_when(
      # No direct estimate: treat as maximum uncertainty.
      is.na(direct_estimate) ~ sampling_variance_ceiling,
      # Missing or tiny variances get the same lower bound.
      is.na(variance) ~ sampling_variance_floor,
      TRUE ~ pmax(variance, sampling_variance_floor)
    )
  ) |>
  arrange(wave_year, area_id)

2 Fit Models
Each model uses the direct estimate as the response. The sampling variance from the direct-estimation workbook is passed to INLA as known observation-level uncertainty, so cells with noisy direct estimates receive less weight.
We will fit five cumulative models:








Model
Name
Specifications




M0
Baseline
Intercept plus independent area effect


M1
+Temporal
M0 plus temporal random walk


M2
+Core predictors
M1 plus population density and no-car households


M3
+All predictors
M2 plus economic activities (full-time students, semi-routine/routine occupation, WFH)


M4
+Spatial
M3 plus spatial structure among MSOA adjacency



We define the model specifications and fit each one to the direct estimates using INLA.

m0_formula <- direct_estimate ~
  1 +
  f(area_iid_id, model = "iid")

m1_formula <- direct_estimate ~
  1 +
  f(area_iid_id, model = "iid") +
  f(year_id, model = "rw1", constr = TRUE)

m2_formula <- direct_estimate ~
  cov_population_density +
  cov_share_no_car_households +
  f(area_iid_id, model = "iid") +
  f(year_id, model = "rw1", constr = TRUE)

m3_formula <- direct_estimate ~
  cov_population_density +
  cov_share_no_car_households +
  cov_share_work_from_home +
  cov_share_students +
  cov_share_routine_semiroutine +
  f(area_iid_id, model = "iid") +
  f(year_id, model = "rw1", constr = TRUE)

m4_formula <- direct_estimate ~
  cov_population_density +
  cov_share_no_car_households +
  cov_share_work_from_home +
  cov_share_students +
  cov_share_routine_semiroutine +
  f(
    area_spatial_id,
    model = "bym2",
    graph = spatial_graph_file,
    scale.model = TRUE,
    constr = TRUE
  ) +
  f(year_id, model = "rw1", constr = TRUE)

model_formulas <- list(
  "M0 Baseline" = m0_formula,
  "M1 +Temporal" = m1_formula,
  "M2 +Core predictors" = m2_formula,
  "M3 +All predictors" = m3_formula,
  "M4 +Spatial" = m4_formula
)

fit_fh_model <- function(formula) {
  INLA::inla(
    formula = formula,
    family = "gaussian",
    data = model_data,
    scale = 1 / model_data$sampling_variance,
    control.family = list(
      hyper = list(
        prec = list(initial = 0, fixed = TRUE)
      )
    ),
    control.predictor = list(compute = TRUE),
    control.compute = list(dic = TRUE, waic = TRUE),
    verbose = FALSE
  )
}

model_order <- names(model_formulas)
fh_fits <- lapply(model_formulas, fit_fh_model)

At this point the result is just a named list of fitted INLA models. We will collate the fitted values into one results table together with their original direct estimates and sampling variances.


Code

output_cols <- c(
  "domain_id",
  "wave_year",
  "msoa_name",
  "direct_estimate",
  "variance",
  "n"

model_output_frame <- select(model_data, all_of(output_cols))

# Extract fitted values from each model and bind them to the frame
fh_result_tables <- purrr::map2(
  fh_fits,
  names(fh_fits),
  function(fit, model_name) {
    fitted_values <- tibble::as_tibble(fit$summary.fitted.values)

    model_results <- bind_cols(model_output_frame, fitted_values)

    transmute(
      model_results,
      model = model_name,
      across(all_of(output_cols)),
      fh_estimate = .data$mean,
      fh_variance = .data$sd^2,
      has_direct = !is.na(.data$direct_estimate)
    )
  }
)

# Stack model outputs and set display order

fh_results <- mutate(
  fh_results,
  model = factor(.data$model, levels = model_order)
)

title: Bayesian Fay-Herriot model
text:
3 Compare Models

3.1 Assess modelled shrinkage from direct estimates
We start by comparing the direct estimates with M0, the baseline Fay-Herriot model. M0 has no area predictors, no temporal term, and no spatial structure. It shows what partial pooling alone does: MSOA-years with high direct-estimate variance contain less local information, so M0 pulls them toward its baseline prediction based on the intercept and independent MSOA random effects.

Because the Bayesian FH model estimates a posterior distribution, cells with missing direct estimates or zero/missing variance can still receive a model-based estimate, reported as a posterior mean with associated uncertainty. This is a benefit of the Bayesian approach in small area estimation where there is sparse or no direct survey information.

Next, we compare the contribution of adding extra information. WAIC, returned by INLA, is a global predictive-fit measure: Lower values indicate better expected prediction after penalising model complexity.

M0 is understandably weaker than the structured models because it has no predictors (-636.6415). When predictors are added, the model updates the expected value for each MSOA-year. Unstable direct estimates are then pulled more strongly toward those updated model predictions, which can improve local accuracy when the predictors are relevant.

3.3 Temporal and spatial effects
The contribution of the temporal and spatial effects on the model prediction can be exmined through two diagnostic outputs by INLA:

tau is the inverse of variance of random effects, both spatil and temporal. A higher value means the random effect varies less.
phi is the share of the BYM2 spatial random-effect variance assigned to the structured spatial component as opposed to the unstructured one. A value of 0.5 means the area random-effect variance is split roughly equally between the structured and unstructured components.

The temporal effect’s tau is high (6091.734), which means the model estimates only small differences between the three survey waves. The effect is still useful to include because it lets the model account for wave-to-wave changes insteading of treating survey responses from all waves as one.

3.2 Assessing Temporal and spatial effects
The contribution of the temporal and spatial effects on the model prediction can be exmined through two diagnostic outputs by INLA:

tau is the inverse of variance of random effects, both spatil and temporal. A higher value means the random effect varies less.
phi is the share of the BYM2 spatial random-effect variance assigned to the structured spatial component as opposed to the unstructured one. A value of 0.5 means the area random-effect variance is split roughly equally between the structured and unstructured components.

The temporal effect’s tau is high (6091.734), which means the model estimates only small differences between the three survey waves. The effect is still useful to include because it lets the model account for wave-to-wave changes insteading of treating survey responses from all waves as one.

Before fitting the models, we create a consistent numeric index for each MSOA and survey year. These indices are used by INLA to attach random effects to the correct area and period.

area_levels <- sort(unique(model_data_raw[["domain_id"]]))
year_levels <- sort(unique(model_data_raw[["wave_year"]]))

area_index <- tibble::tibble(
  domain_id = area_levels,
  area_id = seq_along(area_levels)
)

year_index <- tibble::tibble(
  wave_year = year_levels,
  year_id = seq_along(year_levels)
)

To include a spatial random effect, we also need an adjacency graph .adj as input. We use Queen contiguity, where two MSOAs are treated as neighbours if their boundaries touch at either an edge or a point. The boundary file is sorted using area_index so that the graph order matches the area IDs used in the modelling data.


msoa_boundaries_sorted <- msoa_boundaries |>
  dplyr::inner_join(area_index, by = "domain_id") |>
  dplyr::arrange(.data$area_id)

msoa_neighbours <- spdep::poly2nb(
  msoa_boundaries_sorted,
  queen = TRUE,
  row.names = msoa_boundaries_sorted$domain_id
)

spatial_graph_file <- tempfile(fileext = ".adj")

spdep::nb2INLA(
  file = spatial_graph_file,
  nb = msoa_neighbours
)

We then assemble the modelling data. The models use two area-level random-effect structures, so we create separate INLA index variables:

area_iid_id indexes the unstructured, independent area effect.
area_spatial_id indexes the structured spatial area effect, which uses the adjacency graph.

Lastly, the sampling variance also needs careful handling before fitting the FH models with INLA, because the extent to which the noisy direct estimates will be stablised depends on their sampling variances.

Because the outcome is binary (1 for walking daily, 0 otherwise), small MSOA-year samples can produce direct estimates with very low or zero variance. If untreated, these MSOA-year small areas would be treated by the model as overly precise. To avoid this, we apply a minimum sampling variance floor that is the 5% quantile.
For MSOA-year small areas without a direct estimate and as a result no variance, we assign maximum sampling variance, signalling the high uncertainty. Their estimates will be the model prediction.


sampling_variance_floor <- quantile(
  model_data_raw$variance[model_data_raw$variance > 0],
  probs = 0.05,
  na.rm = TRUE,
  names = FALSE
)

sampling_variance_ceiling <- max(
  model_data_raw$variance[model_data_raw$variance > 0],
  na.rm = TRUE
)

model_data <- model_data_raw |>
  left_join(area_index, by = "domain_id") |>
  left_join(year_index, by = "wave_year") |>
  mutate(
    area_iid_id = area_id,
    area_spatial_id = area_id,
    sampling_variance = case_when(
      # No direct estimate: treat as maximum uncertainty.
      is.na(direct_estimate) ~ sampling_variance_ceiling,
      # Missing or tiny variances get the same lower bound.
      is.na(variance) ~ sampling_variance_floor,
      TRUE ~ pmax(variance, sampling_variance_floor)
    )
  ) |>
  arrange(wave_year, area_id)
